planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: Melissa Burch was certified by the American Camellia Society in January 2026 (Honorarium Certificate No. 7) as an originated Camellia japonica from breeder Pat B. Johnson. As with most japonica cultivars, grow it in humus-rich, acidic, consistently moist but well-drained soil under high or dappled shade, mulching to protect its shallow root system through summer heat. Because this cultivar was only just certified, detailed flower color and form have not yet been published outside the ACS record, so growers should consult the Society's own certificate archive for identification.
sources: ACS Honorarium/In Memoriam Camellia Cultivar Certification Records (certified January 2026)

directions: Pat's Bouffant is a Camellia japonica bred by Pat B. Johnson and certified by the American Camellia Society in January 2026 (Honorarium Certificate No. 8). Its playful name suggests a densely ruffled, full-petaled bloom in keeping with the 'bouffant' hairstyle reference, though the Society's record does not yet publish an official color or form description. Give it the same treatment as other japonica cultivars: acidic, moisture-retentive soil, partial shade, and a thick mulch layer to keep roots cool through the Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Jacob Icard was bred by Pat B. Johnson and certified as a named Camellia japonica by the American Camellia Society in January 2026 (Honorarium Certificate No. 9). Treat it like other japonica cultivars: plant in fall or early spring in acidic, well-drained soil amended with organic matter, and site it where it receives bright shade or filtered morning sun with protection from harsh afternoon exposure. Mulch well and water deeply but infrequently to encourage the deep root system camellias need to withstand Gulf Coast summers.
sources: ACS Honorarium/In Memoriam Camellia Cultivar Certification Records (certified January 2026)

directions: Elegans Becky Root was certified as a named Camellia japonica by the American Camellia Society in January 2026 (Honorarium Certificate No. 10); the Society's record lists no originator for this selection. The 'Elegans' portion of the name suggests a connection to the historic Chandler's Elegans lineage of camellias, but no verified parentage has been published, so that link should be treated as unconfirmed. Grow it under the same regimen as other japonica selections: acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, partial shade, and a steady but not soggy moisture supply through the growing season.
sources: ACS Honorarium/In Memoriam Camellia Cultivar Certification Records (certified January 2026)

directions: Tom Johnson is a Camellia japonica bred by Pat B. Johnson and certified by the American Camellia Society in April 2026 (Honorarium Certificate No. 11); it shares its name with, but is botanically unrelated to, the well-known Tom Johnson bearded iris. Plant in fall or early spring in acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil in dappled or partial shade, mulching to insulate the root zone. As with other recently certified camellias, published flower-form details are still limited outside the Society's own certificate record.
sources: ACS Honorarium/In Memoriam Camellia Cultivar Certification Records (certified April 2026)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; hybrid parentage may be somewhat less cold-tolerant than pure Camellia japonica.

directions: Sarah Docter-Williams was certified by the American Camellia Society in April 2026 (Honorarium Certificate No. 12) and bred by Pat B. Johnson; ACS records it specifically as a non-reticulata hybrid rather than a pure Camellia japonica or sasanqua. Because its exact species parentage beyond 'non-reticulata hybrid' is not published, treat its cold tolerance conservatively and site it in a sheltered, partially shaded spot with acidic, well-drained soil. Mulch heavily and water consistently during establishment, as is standard for interspecific camellia hybrids.
sources: ACS Honorarium/In Memoriam Camellia Cultivar Certification Records (certified April 2026)

Johnson and certified by the American Camellia Society in February 2026 (Honorarium Certificate No. 14) as a named Camellia japonica, honoring the name shared with the famous country singer rather than describing the plant itself. Grow it under standard japonica culture: acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, bright shade or morning sun, and a deep organic mulch to protect roots from summer heat. As a very recently certified selection, its flower description is not yet widely documented beyond the ACS record.

Grow it on the standard japonica regimen: moist but well-drained, acidic soil enriched with organic matter, partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and a generous mulch layer to buffer root temperature swings. Being a newly certified cultivar, detailed public descriptions of its bloom are limited to the Society's own certification materials at this time.

As with most recent ACS honorarium selections, a detailed flower-form description is not yet broadly published outside the Society's own records.

directions: Royal James Wilmot is a Camellia japonica originated by C. M. and Lillian Gordy and certified by the American Camellia Society in January 2024 under its Honorarium/In Memoriam program. Grow it under standard japonica culture: acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, partial shade, and a protective mulch layer over the root zone.

Flower color and form for this selection are not yet documented in widely available nursery or horticultural references beyond the ACS certification record.
sources: ACS Honorarium/In Memoriam Camellia Cultivar Certification Records (certified January 2024)

directions: Worthy's Legacy is a Camellia japonica originated by Lionel Worthy and certified by the American Camellia Society in September 2024 under its Honorarium/In Memoriam program. As its commemorative name suggests, it was registered to preserve a breeder's work for future gardeners rather than for a particular marketed trait, so grow it as a specialist collector's selection. Standard japonica care applies: acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil, partial shade, consistent moisture, and a protective mulch layer through summer heat.
